BARCELONA, Spain -- Barcelona are ready for twice world player of the year Ronaldinho to move on, said club president Joan Laporta. Ronaldinho is expected to leave Barcelona this summer after struggling for form last season. Laporta told the Catalan TV3 station that the Brazilian midfielder, who struggled with injuries and poor form last season, needed new challenges in his career. "When the wheel turns, it's normal that the key figures leave," Laporta said. "I would like Ronaldinho to be given a great send-off so that he is remembered for all he has given us and that if he didn't do any more it was because the circumstances wouldn't allow it. "Last year, we thought that it might be the year to sell him, but given his enthusiasm and the appreciation that a club like Barcelona needs to have, we decided to let him stay on. Things haven't turned out the way he wanted them to." Laporta recognized that it might not be easy to sell Ronaldinho, who suffered a series of injury and fitness problems this season and made the starting line-up in only 13 of 38 league matches. Ronaldinho last played for Barcelona in the 2-1 loss at home to Villarreal on March 9, has suffered muscle pain in his right leg been out of action ever since. AC Milan showed an interest in signing him and his brother Robert De Assis said personal terms had been agreed. But the clubs failed to reach agreement over a transfer fee. After a second successive season without a trophy Barcelona announced on May 7 that Rijkaard would leave at the end of the season and be replaced by former player Josep Guardiola. "We decided that if Frank did not continue then we would choose Guardiola because Pep possessed the necessary humility," said Laporta. "We didn't think about coaches like Mourinho or (Rafa) Benitez, who are both great coaches, but aren't right for Barcelona. So we told Rijkaard that when he left Guardiola would take his place." Barca's arch-rivals Real Madrid, who lifted another Spanish title this season, have signed their first newcomer for the next campaign by paying a reported 10 million euros ($15.5 million) for Argentine defender Ezequiel Garay from Racing Santander. Marca newspaper said the 21-year-old Argentine had signed a six-year contract. Meanwhile, reports that Real could be making a move for Manchester United's Cristiano Ronaldo were dismissed by coach Bernd Schuster. "I prefer to spend my time talking about things that have some bearing to reality," he told a press conference. Marca had reported that Real were still interested in buying Ronaldo who has put off all talk of his future until after the Champions League final.

**BARCELONA, Spain** — FC Barcelona are prepared to part ways with two-time FIFA World Player of the Year Ronaldinho, club president Joan Laporta has confirmed. 

The Brazilian playmaker is widely expected to depart the Camp Nou this summer following a frustrating campaign marred by injuries and inconsistent form. Speaking to Catalan broadcaster TV3, Laporta explained that the midfielder requires a fresh challenge at this stage of his career.

"When the wheel turns, it is natural for key figures to move on," Laporta stated. "I would like Ronaldinho to receive a fitting send-off so he is remembered for everything he gave us, understanding that if he could not offer more, it was simply because circumstances did not allow it. Last year, we considered selling him, but given his enthusiasm and the respect a club like Barcelona must show, we chose to retain him. Unfortunately, things have not unfolded as he had hoped."

Laporta acknowledged that facilitating Ronaldinho's departure may not be straightforward. The 28-year-old struggled with ongoing fitness setbacks this season, featuring in the starting lineup for just 13 of Barcelona’s 38 league matches. His final appearance came in a 2–1 home defeat against Villarreal on March 9, after which a right leg muscle injury sidelined him for the remainder of the campaign. 

AC Milan expressed strong interest in securing his signature, and the player's brother and agent, Roberto de Assis, confirmed that personal terms had been agreed upon. However, the two clubs ultimately failed to reach an agreement on a transfer fee.

Ronaldinho's pending departure comes amid broader changes at the club. Following a second consecutive season without silverware, Barcelona announced on May 7 that manager Frank Rijkaard will step down at the end of the campaign, to be replaced by former club captain Josep "Pep" Guardiola.

"We decided that if Frank were not to continue, Guardiola would be our choice because Pep possesses the requisite humility," Laporta explained. "We did not consider managers like [José] Mourinho or Rafa Benítez; while both are exceptional coaches, they do not fit the Barcelona ethos. Consequently, we informed Rijkaard that Guardiola would succeed him upon his exit."

Meanwhile, Barcelona’s arch-rivals Real Madrid—having recently clinched another La Liga title—have already made their first acquisition for the upcoming campaign. The capital club reportedly paid €10 million ($15.5 million) to sign 21-year-old Argentine defender Ezequiel Garay from Racing Santander, with sports daily *Marca* reporting that he has signed a six-year contract.

Conversely, Real Madrid manager Bernd Schuster swiftly dismissed media reports linking the club with a blockbuster move for Manchester United’s Cristiano Ronaldo. 

"I prefer to spend my time discussing matters grounded in reality," Schuster told reporters during a press conference. *Marca* had reported that Real remained intent on acquiring Ronaldo, who has postponed all discussions regarding his future until after the upcoming Champions League final.

A seismic shift is underway in Spanish football as the 2007–08 La Liga season draws to a close. The biggest news out of the Camp Nou is the end of Frank Rijkaard’s five-year tenure as Barcelona head coach. Club president Joan Laporta confirmed that the Dutch manager, who led Barcelona to back-to-back La Liga titles and the 2006 UEFA Champions League trophy, will step down at the end of the season. 

Rijkaard will be replaced by 37-year-old Pep Guardiola, the iconic former Barcelona midfielder who has spent the current season managing the club's 'B' team. Guardiola’s appointment represents a bold gamble by Laporta, promoting a young coach with no top-flight managerial experience to restore discipline and tactical rigor to a squad that has visibly drifted over the past two years.

"Frank Rijkaard has made history with us," Laporta said during a press conference in Barcelona. "However, the results have not gone our way, and we agree that a cycle has come to an end. Pep Guardiola has the knowledge, the enthusiasm, and the commitment to lead this new project."

### Laporta Confirms Ronaldinho’s Imminent Departure

Accompanying the managerial change is the clearest signal yet that Barcelona's playing staff will undergo a radical purge. Speaking to Spanish media, Laporta publicly acknowledged for the first time that two-time FIFA World Player of the Year Ronaldinho is on his way out of the club.

Ronaldinho, 28, has endured a dismal, injury-plagued season characterized by fitness concerns and off-the-field controversies. Having featured sparingly in recent months, the Brazilian superstar was noticeably absent from Barcelona’s embarrassing 4-1 loss to Real Madrid at the Santiago Bernabéu earlier this month.

Laporta admitted that both the club and the player agree a change of scenery is necessary. 

"Ronaldinho needs a new challenge," Laporta stated in a radio interview. "When a cycle ends, it is normal that the players who spearheaded that era move on. We will work to ensure he receives a send-off worthy of everything he has given Barcelona, but it is best for all parties if he continues his career elsewhere."

AC Milan have emerged as the frontrunners to sign the Brazilian, though Premier League side Manchester City—backed by Thai businessman Thaksin Shinawatra—are also reportedly preparing a lucrative bid. Laporta hinted that fellow star forward Samuel Eto'o and Portuguese playmaker Deco may also be allowed to leave as Guardiola prepares to rebuild the team around Lionel Messi.

### Champions Real Madrid Target Market Upgrades

In stark contrast to the turmoil in Catalonia, Real Madrid are celebrating their 31st league title after a dominant season under Bernd Schuster. However, club president Ramón Calderón and sporting director Predrag Mijatović are not resting on their laurels, setting their sights on high-profile summer additions to build a squad capable of winning the Champions League.

Madrid have already secured one of La Liga’s brightest young defensive talents, agreeing to a €10 million deal with Racing Santander for 21-year-old Argentine center-back Ezequiel Garay, who is expected to spend next season on loan before fully integrating into the squad.

Beyond Garay, *Los Blancos* are heavily linked with Ajax striker Klaas-Jan Huntelaar and Hamburg's Rafael van der Vaart. However, the worst-kept secret in the capital is Madrid’s audacious, record-breaking pursuit of Manchester United winger Cristiano Ronaldo. Reports in Spain suggest Calderón is prepared to break the bank for the Portuguese star, despite fierce resistance from Sir Alex Ferguson.

While Real Madrid look to add firepower to an already championship-winning side, Barcelona face a summer of radical reconstruction. With Guardiola at the helm and Ronaldinho set to depart, the balance of power in Spanish football is entering a fascinating new chapter.

Here is a summary of the key transfer news and sagas from La Liga during the summer of 2008:

---

### 1. FC Barcelona: Pep Guardiola’s Revolution Begins
After a trophy-less 2007–08 season under Frank Rijkaard, 37-year-old Pep Guardiola was appointed head coach and immediately began dismantling the "Galáctico" culture in Catalonia.

*   **The Big Departures:** Guardiola famously announced that Ronaldinho, Deco, and Samuel Eto'o were not in his plans. 
    *   **Ronaldinho** was sold to AC Milan for €21 million, marking the end of an era.
    *   **Deco** moved to Chelsea to join Luiz Felipe Scolari.
    *   *Note:* Samuel Eto'o convinced Pep during pre-season to let him stay—a decision that proved crucial to Barca's eventual Treble win.
    *   Gianluca Zambrotta returned to Italy (AC Milan), and Giovani dos Santos was sold to Tottenham Hotspur.
*   **Key Arrivals:** Barcelona spent heavily to rebuild:
    *   **Dani Alves** arrived from Sevilla for around €35 million, making him one of the most expensive defenders in history at the time.
    *   **Gerard Piqué** was brought back from Manchester United for a bargain €5 million.
    *   **Seydou Keita** (Sevilla), **Martin Cáceres** (Villarreal), and **Alexander Hleb** (Arsenal) were also signed.

---

### 2. Real Madrid: The CR7 Saga & Deadline Day Chaos
Real Madrid entered the summer as back-to-back La Liga champions, but President Ramón Calderón focused almost all his energy on one target: **Cristiano Ronaldo**.

*   **The Cristiano Ronaldo Saga:** Madrid spent months publicly courting the Manchester United star. United manager Sir Alex Ferguson famously balked at Madrid's tactics, stating he "wouldn't sell that mob a virus." Ronaldo ultimately stayed in Manchester for one more year, leaving Madrid empty-handed late in the window.
*   **Robinho’s Dramatic Exit:** Upset at being offered as a potential bargain chip in the Cristiano Ronaldo chase, Brazilian winger Robinho demanded to leave. On deadline day (September 1), expecting a move to Chelsea, he was instead sold for £32.5 million to **Manchester City**, who had just been taken over by the Abu Dhabi United Group.
*   **The Only Major Signing:** Real Madrid’s primary incoming transfer was Dutch playmaker **Rafael van der Vaart** from Hamburger SV for €13 million. They also recalled Rubén de la Red and Javi García.

---

### 3. Valencia: Keeping the Euro 2008 Heroes
Fresh off Spain’s triumph at Euro 2008, Spanish stars were in high demand. Valencia was suffering from severe financial trouble, leading to rumors that their top stars would be liquidated.

*   **David Villa:** Madrid and Chelsea heavily pursued the Euro 2008 top scorer, but Valencia pulled out of negotiations, keeping Villa at the Mestalla.
*   **David Silva:** Linked to Barcelona and several Premier League clubs, Silva ultimately signed a new contract extension to stay at Valencia.

---

### 4. Atlético Madrid: Rebuilding for the Champions League
Having finished 4th in 2007–08, Atlético Madrid spent heavily to build a squad capable of competing in the UEFA Champions League alongside young superstar Sergio "Kun" Agüero and Diego Forlán.

*   **Key Arrivals:**
    *   **John Heitinga** (Defender, from Ajax)
    *   **Tomáš Ujfaluši** (Defender, from Fiorentina)
    *   **Gregory Coupet** (Goalkeeper, from Lyon)
    *   **Paulo Assunção** (Midfielder, from Porto)
    *   **Florent Sinama-Pongolle** (Forward, from Recreativo Huelva)

---

### 5. Sevilla: Forced Rebuilding
Sevilla, a dominant force in the mid-2000s, saw their squad stripped of key leaders:

*   **Out:** **Dani Alves** and **Seydou Keita** were sold to Barcelona, while midfielder **Christian Poulsen** moved to Juventus.
*   **In:** Sevilla re-invested the funds into players like defender **Sébastien Squillaci** (Lyon), midfielder **Romaric** (Le Mans), and left-back **Fernando Navarro** (Mallorca).

---

### Summary of the Impact
The mid-2008 transfer window fundamentally reshaped European football. Real Madrid’s failure to sign Cristiano Ronaldo led to a relatively quiet window that left them unprepared for Barcelona's resurgence. Meanwhile, Pep Guardiola's precise, bold transfer moves laid the exact groundwork for FC Barcelona's legendary **2008–09 Treble-winning season**.

The Brazilian magician, who arrived in 2003 and spearheaded Barcelona’s rise back to the top of European football with two La Liga titles and the 2006 Champions League, is officially being put up for sale.

Confirming the superstar's departure, Laporta was solemn but firm: "Ronaldinho needs a new challenge. When a cycle ends, it is because of natural causes, and it is best for both parties to part ways. We will always be grateful to him for bringing the smile back to the Camp Nou, but the team's dynamic requires a fresh start."

Guardiola, sitting alongside Laporta and sporting director Txiki Begiristain, wasted no time in establishing his authority. The incoming manager dropped a bombshell by revealing that Ronaldinho, along with fellow high-profile stars Deco and Samuel Eto’o, are not in his plans for the upcoming season.

"We are planning the squad without Ronaldinho, Deco, and Eto'o," Guardiola stated calmly, sending shockwaves through the press room. "It is time for a reset. If I felt that Ronaldinho wanted to return to being the player he was, I might reconsider, but the situation has changed. I want a committed, disciplined squad where the team comes before any individual."

The decision marks a tragic end to Ronaldinho's brilliant five-year tenure in Catalonia. Once considered the undisputed best player on the planet, the Ballon d'Or winner’s final season was plagued by injuries, fitness issues, and rumors of an uncontrolled nightlife, leading to a breakdown in his relationship with the club’s hierarchy.

With Ronaldinho on his way out—with Manchester City and AC Milan reported as prospective suitors—Guardiola is expected to build his new-look team around 20-year-old Argentine prodigy Lionel Messi and a core of academy talents, including Xavi, Andrés Iniesta, and Carles Puyol.

The reaction among the *Culés* (Barcelona supporters) is deeply divided. While many applaud Laporta's ruthlessness in clearing out the bloated superstar culture, others fear that handing the reins to an inexperienced manager like Guardiola while casting off a generational talent like Ronaldinho could backfire spectacularly.

One thing is certain: the 'Joga Bonito' era of Frank Rijkaard and Ronaldinho is officially over. The Pep Guardiola revolution at FC Barcelona has begun.

# The Revolution of 2008: Why Barcelona Sold Ronaldinho, Chose Guardiola, and Redefined Modern Football

In the summer of 2008, FC Barcelona stood at a terrifying crossroads. Just two years removed from winning the 2006 UEFA Champions League, the club was in freefall. Complacency had poisoned the dressing room, the team had just finished a humiliating 18 points behind arch-rivals Real Madrid in La Liga, and the squad's indisputable crown jewel, Ronaldinho, had transformed from the best player on the planet into a symbol of decadence and decline.

What followed in the summer of 2008 was one of the most audacious cultural and tactical overhauls in sports history. By choosing a novice manager in Pep Guardiola, ruthlessly casting aside Ronaldinho, and restructuring the club's hierarchy, Barcelona did not just rebuild—they laid the foundation for the greatest club side ever assembled.

Here is the comprehensive story of how Barcelona dismantled an empire to build a dynasty.

---

## Part I: The Fall of the House of Rijkaard and Ronaldinho

To understand why Ronaldinho was sold, one must understand the environment that allowed his decline. 

Between 2003 and 2006, Frank Rijkaard and Ronaldinho saved modern Barcelona. President Joan Laporta’s project took off precisely because Ronaldinho brought joy, magic, and trophies back to the Camp Nou. However, Rijkaard’s management style was built on high trust and low tactical rigidity. While this laissez-faire approach allowed Ronaldinho’s flair to flourish, it proved fatal once the team lost its hunger.

Following the 2006 Champions League triumph in Paris, a slow rot set in. Ronaldinho’s penchant for Barcelona’s nightlife became an open secret. Late-night partying, missed training sessions, and visible weight gain replaced the mesmerizing runs that had once earned him a standing ovation from Real Madrid fans at the Santiago Bernabéu. 

By the 2007–08 season, the team was adrift:
* **Tactical Stagnation:** The team lacked pressing, work ethic, and dynamic movement.
* **Loss of Discipline:** Key stars like Ronaldinho and Deco operated under their own rules, creating resentment within the squad.
* **The Humiliation:** The ultimate breaking point arrived in May 2008. Barcelona was forced to perform the *pasillo* (guard of honor) for freshly crowned champions Real Madrid at the Bernabéu, after which they were soundly beaten 4–1.

Rijkaard’s gentle touch could no longer command the dressing room. His departure at the end of the season was an inevitability.

---

## Part II: The Managerial Crossroads: Why Pep Over Mourinho?

With Rijkaard outgoing, Joan Laporta and sporting director Txiki Begiristain needed a new manager. The board was sharply divided over two drastically different candidates: **José Mourinho** and **Pep Guardiola**.

### The Case for José Mourinho
Mourinho was the world’s most coveted manager. Fresh off massive success at Porto and Chelsea, he was a proven winner, a master tactician, and crucially, he *wanted* the job. Mourinho had worked at Barcelona in the late 1990s under Bobby Robson and Louis van Gaal and knew the club intimately. He even prepared a detailed PowerPoint presentation for the Barca board, outlining how he would restructure the squad and re-energize the tactical system. 

Many board members favored Mourinho because he offered an immediate guarantee of trophies and possessed the tough-guy persona required to tame a chaotic dressing room.

### The Choice: Pep Guardiola
Despite Mourinho’s stellar resume, legendary former player and club patriarch **Johan Cruyff** advised Laporta to look elsewhere. Cruyff argued that Mourinho’s confrontational personality, pragmatic brand of football, and tendency to create media circuses conflicted with Barcelona’s identity.

Instead, Cruyff and Begiristain advocated for Pep Guardiola. 

At the time, Guardiola was a massive gamble. He had zero top-flight managerial experience, having spent just one season managing Barcelona B in the Spanish fourth division (Tercera División). However, Guardiola offered three things Mourinho could not:
1. **Purity of Philosophy:** Pep was an obsessive student of Cruyffian positional play (*Juego de Posición*).
2. **Deep Club Identity:** As a former captain and ball-boy, Pep understood the socio-political fabric of Barcelona.
3. **Uncompromising Discipline:** Having coached the young B-team players (like Sergio Busquets and Pedro), Pep knew that success required insane work ethic, tactical rigour, and a clean culture.

Laporta took the ultimate risk, rejected Mourinho, and promoted Guardiola to the first team.

---

## Part III: The Cold Decision: Selling Ronaldinho

Upon taking the job in June 2008, Guardiola held his iconic first press conference. He delivered a bombshell that rocked Spanish football:

> *"We are planning the squad without Ronaldinho, Deco, and Samuel Eto'o. If they were at their best, they would be with us, but the time has come for a reset."*

*(Note: Eto'o eventually convinced Pep to let him stay for one more season through sheer work ethic in pre-season, but Ronaldinho and Deco were instantly cast out.)*

The decision to sell Ronaldinho—who was only 28 years old—was driven by three main factors:

### 1. Protecting the Crown Prince: Lionel Messi
This was the most critical factor. Lionel Messi looked up to Ronaldinho as a big brother. They were deeply fond of one another, and Ronaldinho had mentored the young Argentine during his breakout years. However, the Barcelona hierarchy grew terrified that Ronaldinho’s nocturnal lifestyle and poor professional habits would rub off on Messi. If Messi was to fulfill his potential as the world's best player, Ronaldinho’s influence had to be removed.

### 2. A Shift in Culture: System Over Individualism
Guardiola believed that no single player could be bigger than the collective. Ronaldinho relied on individual genius, spontaneous magic, and physical superiority. Guardiola demanded tactical synchronization, high-intensity pressing, and obsessive dedication to detail. Ronaldinho’s physical decline meant he could no longer execute the intense off-ball work Pep required.

### 3. The Transfer to AC Milan
In July 2008, Ronaldinho was sold to AC Milan for approximately €24 million—a fraction of what he would have commanded two years prior. Though his exit was heartbreaking for fans who remembered his peak, it was a necessary sacrifice to usher in the new age.

---

## Part IV: What Was Real Madrid Doing at the Time?

To fully appreciate Barcelona's summer of 2008, one must look across the divide at Real Madrid. 

While Barcelona was tearing down its foundation, Real Madrid was feeling comfortable—perhaps overly so. Under President Ramón Calderón and manager Bernd Schuster, Madrid had just won back-to-back La Liga titles (2006–07 and 2007–08). 

### The "Dutch Invasion" Strategy
Real Madrid’s transfer market policy at the time was heavily focused on assembling a core of top-tier Dutch talent, alongside promising South Americans. 

Between 2006 and 2008, Real Madrid signed:
* **Ruud van Nistelrooy** (2006)
* **Wesley Sneijder** (2007)
* **Arjen Robben** (2007)
* **Royston Drenthe** (2007)
* **Rafael van der Vaart** (Summer 2008)
* **Gonzalo Higuaín** & **Marcelo** (Winter 2007)

In the summer of 2008, while Barcelona was appointing Pep and clearing out icons, Real Madrid’s summer was surprisingly quiet. Their marquee signing was Rafael van der Vaart from Hamburger SV for €13 million. Madrid believed their squad was already vastly superior to Barcelona's and did not anticipate the radical transformation occurring in Catalonia.

Furthermore, Madrid spent much of the summer of 2008 publicly chasing Manchester United's **Cristiano Ronaldo**. They failed to land him that year (he would stay in Manchester until 2009), leaving Madrid’s management somewhat distracted and overly confident in their domestic dominance.

---

## Part V: The Legacy of the 2008 Decisions

The summer of 2008 remains a masterclass in strategic sports management. 

By removing Ronaldinho and installing Guardiola:
* **Lionel Messi was liberated.** Handed the number 10 shirt, moved into the "false nine" role, and paired with a professional, hyper-disciplined squad, Messi evolved into the greatest player in history.
* **La Masia flourished.** Pep immediately integrated Xavi and Andrés Iniesta as the central nervous system of the team, while promoting Sergio Busquets and Pedro from the B-team.
* **The Sextuple:** In Pep's very first season (2008–09), Barcelona achieved the unthinkable, winning La Liga, the Copa del Rey, and the Champions League—eventually winning an unprecedented six trophies in a single calendar year (the Sextuple). Included in that run was a famous 6–2 destruction of Real Madrid at the Bernabéu.

Real Madrid was caught so off-guard by Barcelona’s sudden brilliance that Ramón Calderón resigned in early 2009. **Florentino Pérez** returned as Real Madrid president in the summer of 2009, launching the famous *Galácticos 2.0* era (signing Cristiano Ronaldo, Kaká, Karim Benzema, and Xabi Alonso in a single window) purely as an emergency response to the monster Barcelona had created.

## Conclusion

The decision to sell Ronaldinho in 2008 was a terrifying leap into the unknown. It meant parting ways with the global icon who had defined the club's modern identity, placing the keys to the kingdom in the hands of a 37-year-old rookie manager. 

Yet, history proved it to be a stroke of absolute genius. By prioritizing culture, tactical harmony, and the growth of Lionel Messi over past glories, Barcelona transformed a moment of crisis into the dawn of football's greatest dynasty.
